subject: Accounting
title: What Are Liabilities?
description: A fast breakdown of What Are Liabilities? for builders.

hook.text: A business with $5 million in the bank sounds rich—until you see $8 million in debt.

buildup.text: Liabilities are obligations: loans, unpaid bills, wages owed, taxes due.

discovery.text: Current liabilities are due within a year. Long-term ones stretch further out.

twist.text: Some liabilities are good. A smart loan to expand can multiply profits many times over.

climax.text: The key isn't zero debt—it's knowing helpful debt from dangerous debt.

punchline.text: What you owe matters as much as what you own.

quiz.question: What is a current liability?
options: An obligation due within one year

details.summary: Liabilities are obligations a company owes to others that will require future sacrifice of economic resources—typically cash payments. This topic introduces how liabilities are defined, classified by time horizon, and reported on the balance sheet.
details.whyItMatters: Liabilities reveal how much of a company's assets are financed by obligations to others. They directly impact risk, borrowing capacity, and the company's ability to survive downturns.
takeaways: A liability is a present obligation arising from a past event that will require a future economic sacrifice
Current liabilities are settled within one year; non-current liabilities extend beyond one year
The ratio of liabilities to equity (leverage) is a key indicator of financial risk

faq.question: What qualifies as a liability in accounting?
faq.answer: A liability is a present obligation to transfer economic resources (usually cash) due to a past transaction or event. Borrowing money creates a loan payable. Receiving goods from a supplier creates accounts payable. The key test: does the company owe something as a result of a past event?

faq.question: Are all debts considered liabilities?
faq.answer: All debts are liabilities, but not all liabilities are debts. Liabilities also include obligations that aren't traditional borrowing—wages owed to employees, taxes owed to the government, payments received for services not yet delivered (unearned revenue), and warranty obligations.
